Over 45 days since the S&P 500's October 6 high, roughly $6 trillion in market value evaporated amid concerns over massive Big Tech AI capital expenditures (reaching a record $201.9 billion in Q3 2026), negative free cash flow, the end of the "Trump Put" following a Democratic midterm sweep, Fed rate hikes under Chair Warsh, Nvidia's loss of Jensen Huang and a 40% stock decline, AMD chip-smuggling allegations, and liquidity strain from Anthropic's record IPO. Despite this, fundamentals remain strong: S&P 500 Q3 2026 EPS grew 31.9% year-over-year, the strongest in four years, with 13 consecutive quarters of beats. Tech forward P/E has fallen to its lowest since March 2020, with Nvidia at just 9x. Sentiment is at crisis levels—VIX up over 100% from October lows, hedge funds seeing their largest six-week outflow in over a decade—and markets are pricing in an overly pessimistic outcome including aggressive AI regulation and disappointing ROI. The authors view this as a normal correction, not a bubble burst, noting even another 10% decline would remain within a healthy pullback. They caution against calling for a prolonged bear market, see limited downside beyond 30%, and argue risk-reward is becoming attractive for high-quality tech companies with strong balance sheets and accelerating earnings growth. Wilson and Nicholas Lentini, reported that institutional portfolio changes in Q3 2026 were notably smaller than in Q2, based on 13F filings as of September 30, 2026. Large-cap investors added to information technology (+1.3%), health care (+0.5%), and energy (+0.4%), while trimming industrials (-0.8%), consumer discretionary (-0.6%), and utilities (-0.3%). These increases largely tracked sector performance—energy rose 17.2%, IT 7.2%, and health care 6.5%, while utilities fell 12.4% and industrials 9.7%—suggesting passive price-driven weighting rather than aggressive active repositioning. Hedge funds similarly added health care (+0.9%) and IT (+0.8%) and cut industrials (-0.8%) and consumer discretionary (-0.5%); financials were the only sector with a divergence, as hedge funds added 0.3% while all 13F institutions cut 0.2%. Tech remained underweight: IT’s S&P 500 benchmark weight rose to 40%, leaving institutions 1.0% underweight and hedge funds 7.2% underweight, up from 6.3%.

Small caps saw a sharp style shift. The Russell 2000 fell 7.5% in Q3. Small-cap flows moved into health care (+1.1%) and energy (+1.0%), while exiting industrials (-1.1%), IT (-0.6%), and consumer discretionary (-0.6%). Energy staged a dramatic reversal: after being the most heavily sold small-cap sector in Q2 (long-only funds -1.0%, hedge funds -1.3%), hedge funds added 1.3% in Q3, making it their top small-cap addition.
